planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring; Black Jack's purple-black stems and foliage hold their dark color best in lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Black Jack arose as a mutation discovered in a Michigan field of the popular Sedum Matrona and carries the same robust upright habit with even darker coloring. Succulent leaves emerge purple-green in spring and rapidly deepen to a near-black purple that holds through summer heat, topped in late summer by wide, flattened clusters of small star-shaped pink flowers that draw bees and butterflies. Grow in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where strong light intensifies the dark foliage and keeps the thick stems self-supporting without staking. Leave the dried flowerheads standing through winter for structural interest before cutting the clump back in early spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Postman's Pride keeps a compact, bushy habit that rarely needs staking.

directions: Named for the Belgian postal carrier who discovered it in his own garden, Postman's Pride is prized for deep bluish-purple to brownish-purple succulent foliage that holds its color from spring through fall. Masses of red-purple, star-shaped flower clusters open from late summer into fall on a compact, semi-upright plant, drawing honeybees and butterflies at a time when few other perennials are still blooming. It thrives in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade and, once established, needs little supplemental water even through summer dry spells. Divide congested clumps in spring, or take stem or leaf cuttings in early summer to increase stock.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Lynda Windsor forms a tidy, compact clump that pairs well with ornamental grasses.

directions: Lynda Windsor is a compact, moderate-growing border stonecrop whose fleshy foliage emerges deep purple-red in spring and holds strong color through the season. Abundant, wide, deep red flower clusters up to four inches across open from late summer into early autumn atop sturdy, upright stems that rarely need staking. It performs best in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun, where good drainage prevents crown rot over winter. Combine it with silver-foliaged companions or ornamental grasses for contrast, and leave the dried seed heads standing into winter before cutting back in early spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; strong, short stems keep Mr. Goodbud standing through winter without staking.

directions: Bred by Terra Nova Nurseries from Sedum spectabile 'Brilliant' crossed with an unnamed Sedum telephium, Mr. Goodbud produces exceptionally large, 5-6 inch clusters of vivid purple-pink flowers opening from buds that are nearly white, held above red-tinted foliage. Its strong, short stems form a dense, upright clump that resists flopping better than many taller sedums and remains attractive as a standing winter silhouette. Grow in average, dry to medium, well-drained soil in full sun, with tolerance for light shade and considerable drought once roots are established. Late-season blooms make it a magnet for bees, butterflies, and migrating monarchs, and the RHS Award of Garden Merit recognizes its reliable garden performance.

common_name: Blue Pearl Sedum (Blue-Plum Foliage SunSparkler Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Blue Pearl is grown primarily for its foliage color, which holds all season.

directions: A member of Walters Gardens' SunSparkler series bred for foliage-first appeal, Blue Pearl forms a low, spreading mound of thick, bluish-plum leaves that keep their smoky color through the growing season rather than fading with heat. Clusters of pink, star-shaped flowers appear in late summer but are secondary to the foliage display that gives the cultivar its name and lasting garden interest. It thrives in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun and shrugs off heat and drought once established, making it a dependable groundcover for rock gardens, border edges, and container plantings. Shear lightly after flowering if a tighter mat is desired, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Plum Dazzled Sedum (Dark Purple Foliage SunSparkler Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Plum Dazzled forms a mat-like mound of rich plum-purple foliage.

directions: Plum Dazzled is a SunSparkler-series stonecrop selected for its abundance of fleshy, dark purple leaves that form a dense, mat-forming mound and hold their rich color from spring through frost. In late summer, clusters of vibrant pink, star-shaped flowers rise just above the foliage and continue the color display into fall, drawing butterflies and other pollinators. It performs best in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where good drainage and strong light together produce the deepest foliage pigmentation and the sturdiest, most compact habit. Extremely drought-tolerant once rooted in, it suits rock gardens, dry borders, and container combinations, and needs only an occasional light shearing to maintain a tidy mound.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Lime Twister roots readily from broken stem pieces and fills in quickly.

directions: A variegated sport of the popular groundcover sedum Angelina, Lime Twister carries the same needle-like, thumbnail-sized leaves but edged in wide bands of creamy white around a lime-green center. Cool spring and fall temperatures bring out a picotee edge of pink-red along the leaf margins, adding a third color to the already striking foliage display, while sparse rose-pink flowers appear in summer. It spreads into a low, trailing mound over well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun, rooting quickly wherever trailing stems touch soil, and tolerates drought and poor soil with ease once established. Use it to brighten rock gardens, wall crevices, and container edges, trimming back any all-green reversion shoots to keep the variegation strong.

common_name: Green Mantle Sedum (Non-Flowering Bright Green Groundcover Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Green Mantle roots along its spreading stems and fills in quickly as a weed-suppressing mat.

directions: Green Mantle is a vigorous, mat-forming form of two-row stonecrop grown chiefly for its fresh, bright green, semi-evergreen foliage rather than for showy bloom, forming dense rosettes on spreading, rooting stems that knit together into a tight groundcover. Small, star-shaped yellow flowers appear in rounded clusters in summer, adding a light seasonal accent without detracting from the clean foliage effect. It tolerates poor, lean, sheltered sites in full sun and is a favorite for green roof and vertical wall plantings where a uniform green texture is wanted over showy color. Shear back hard every few years if the mat becomes woody at the center, and divide congested sections in spring to renew vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Regarded as one of the best variegated sedums, this low, mat-forming, semi-evergreen selection of orange stonecrop bears fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves edged in creamy white with a pink flush at the margins. Showy clusters of small, golden-yellow, starry flowers open in summer and gradually turn crimson as they fade, adding a second season of color contrast against the pale-edged foliage. It grows well in full sun or partial shade in moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil and tolerates dry sites once established, holding the Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for reliable garden performance. Use it in rock gardens, dry walls, and groundcover plantings where its variegation reads well at close range.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; Atlantis forms tidy, ground-hugging rosettes that spread slowly into a dense mat.

directions: Originating from the volcanic island of Ulleungdo off the Korean coast, Atlantis is a selection of Takeshima stonecrop forming ground-hugging rosettes of thick, dark green leaves broadly margined in creamy yellow. Showy sprays of bright yellow, starry flowers rise on short, thick stems in summer and are attractive to butterflies, adding bloom color to a plant already valued for its variegated foliage. It is tough and cold-hardy, thriving in full sun in average to poor, neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil, and can go long stretches without supplemental water once established. Use it as a front-of-border accent, in rock gardens, or in containers where its bright, cream-edged rosettes stand out against darker-leaved companions.

common_name: Lemonjade Sedum (Citron-Yellow Flowered Rock N Grow Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; Lemonjade forms a compact, mounded clump with unusually bright yellow late-season flowers.

directions: Bred from an open-pollinated cross with Sedum 'Sheila McQueen' as the seed parent, Lemonjade stands out among autumn stonecrops for its large, 5-7 inch panicles of bright citron-yellow flowers rather than the typical pink, opening in early fall above compact, mounded, blue-green foliage. As cold weather sets in, the spent flowerheads take on rosy peach tones, extending seasonal interest well past peak bloom. Grow in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun, where the sturdy, clump-forming habit needs no staking and tolerates heat and drought with ease once established. Part of the Rock 'N Grow collection, it works well in border fronts, rock gardens, and mixed containers alongside darker-flowered sedum cultivars for contrast.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted stem pieces in spring in poor to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Album Superbum roots readily at the nodes and forms a dense mat.

directions: Album Superbum is a white-flowered selection of two-row stonecrop with sprawling, branching stems that root easily at the nodes to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat of thick, toothed, obovate leaves. Clusters of small, star-shaped white flowers cover the foliage in early summer, giving a cleaner, brighter effect than the pink- or red-flowered spurium cultivars more commonly grown. It thrives in poor, dry, even slightly chalky soil in full sun and tolerates partial shade better than many sedums, making it a flexible choice for green roofs, dry walls, and groundcover plantings in mixed light. Once established it needs almost no supplemental water and spreads reliably without becoming invasive, requiring only an occasional trim to keep it within bounds.
sources: Emory Knoll Farms Green Roof Plants

common_name: Kimnach's Pachyphytum (Compact Powder-Blue Bead Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in a lean, gritty cactus mix; let cut surfaces callus for a few days before setting them on the soil surface.

directions: Grow in full sun to bright light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, watering deeply and then allowing the soil to dry out completely before the next watering. Named for Myron Kimnach, longtime director of the Huntington Botanical Gardens, this Oaxacan species forms tight, low clusters of thick, powdery blue-grey leaves that tinge dusky mauve under strong light and cool temperatures. Keep it dry and sheltered from hard frost, as the brittle, heavily-farinose leaves bruise easily and lose their protective bloom with handling.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining mix; older stems trail and are best grown in a raised bed or hanging container.

directions: Grow in full sun in gritty, well-drained succulent mix, soaking thoroughly and then letting the mix dry fully before watering again. Native to central Mexico, this species carries noticeably longer, narrow, cylindrical-to-club-shaped leaves than the compact moonstone-type pachyphytums already in the dataset, coated in a chalky glaucous bloom that ranges from blue-green to lavender-grey. Stems elongate and lean or trail with age, so mature plants are best displayed where their length can spill over a container edge; protect from frost and from overhead watering that can mark the powdery leaf surface.

common_name: Machuca's Pachyphytum (Dense Glaucous White Bead Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or short stem cuttings in spring in a lean, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; allow cut ends to callus before inserting into the mix.

directions: Grow in full sun to bright light in a lean, fast-draining succulent mix, watering thoroughly and then letting the soil dry out completely before rewatering. One of the earliest pachyphytums described from Oaxaca, Mexico, it forms dense, low rosettes of thick, plump leaves coated in a heavy white-grey glaucous bloom that rubs off with handling, so plants are best kept where they will not be brushed against. Small bell-shaped flowers rise on short spikes above the foliage in spring; shelter from hard frost and from wet, poorly drained soil, which quickly rots the fleshy leaves.

common_name: Moonglow Graptoveria (Silvery Frosted Blue Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; as a named hybrid cultivar it does not come true from seed, so propagation is strictly vegetative.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the mix dry out completely before the next watering. This Graptopetalum-Echeveria hybrid forms broad, symmetrical rosettes of thick, powder-coated silvery-blue leaves that take on a pale lavender cast in cooler weather, distinct from the pink-flushed graptoverias already in the dataset. It offsets readily to form clumps and suits dish gardens and mixed succulent containers; bring pots under cover when temperatures approach freezing, since the frosty leaf coating bruises easily and the foliage has little frost tolerance.

common_name: Czechmark Sunny Side Up Weigela (White-and-Yellow Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; the crisp white-and-yellow bicolor bloom develops best with a full day of direct light.

directions: Czechmark Sunny Side Up stands apart from typical pink or red weigelas with crisp white, trumpet-shaped flowers marked by a cheerful yellow throat, produced in unusually heavy quantity along apple-green foliage each spring. Bred as part of the Czech Republic's Czechmark series alongside Czechmark Trilogy, it shares that line's rounded, semi-compact habit and needs no deadheading to keep blooming into early summer. It resists deer and rabbit browsing better than most weigelas and draws bees and hummingbirds to its nectar-rich flowers. Prune right after the main spring flush to shape the plant, since flower buds form on the previous season's wood.

common_name: Show Off Sugar Baby Forsythia (Dwarf Compact Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full to part sun; its tiny mature footprint suits foundation beds and small-space borders where full-size forsythia would overwhelm.

directions: Show Off Sugar Baby is the smallest member of the Show Off series, bred in France for a genuinely dwarf, space-saving habit that still blooms along the entire length of every stem rather than just at the tips. Bright yellow, bell-shaped flowers smother the bare branches in earliest spring ahead of the emerald summer foliage, and the plant needs no pruning to keep its tidy dense form. It tolerates a wide range of soils, shrugs off occasional drought once established, and its flowers hold up well when cut for indoor arrangements. As with all forsythia, flower bud cold-hardiness rather than stem hardiness sets its northern limit.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in average, well-drained soil in full to part sun; its 3-foot mature size fits small landscapes and border fronts where full-size forsythia won't.

directions: Show Off Starlet packs the same highlighter-yellow, densely packed spring bloom that made the Show Off series popular into a dwarf frame only about three feet tall and wide. Flower buds erupt along the full length of every branch rather than clustering at the tips, giving a solid ball of gold color in earliest spring before the leaves emerge. It is very deer-resistant, tolerates black walnut and occasional dry spells once established, and needs little to no pruning to hold its compact rounded shape. Water through the first season to establish; after that, rainfall is usually sufficient in most regions.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; its compact mounded habit fits patio containers and small borders where standard forsythia would sprawl.

directions: Minigold is an older but still widely grown dwarf forsythia, smothering its compact mounded branches in small, deep-yellow, star-shaped flowers from March into May before the foliage emerges. Its diminutive scale, roughly a quarter the size of standard border forsythia, makes it a good fit for patio containers as well as small-space foundation plantings. It tolerates acid to alkaline soils as long as they stay evenly moist and are not too chalky, and needs only light shaping after flowering to maintain its neat form. Like other forsythias, it blooms on old wood, so any pruning should happen immediately after the spring flower display fades.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in reasonably fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil; site in full sun to part shade, with light afternoon shade helping preserve leaf color and prevent scorch in hot climates.

directions: Deutzia gracilis 'Aurea' brings bright golden-yellow-green, lance-shaped foliage to a compact bushy frame, holding its color through the season before loose clusters of fragrant, star-shaped white flowers open from late spring into early summer. The chartreuse foliage makes an effective color echo or contrast plant in mixed shrub borders even outside of bloom time. Protect from late spring frosts, which can damage emerging growth, and avoid letting the soil dry out, since gracilis types perform poorly under drought stress. Propagate from softwood cuttings in summer or hardwood cuttings taken in autumn; prune lightly right after flowering since blooms form on old wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; the purple-flushed buds show best where the shrub gets a half day or more of direct sun.

directions: Joconde is one of the classic Lemoine hybrid deutzias introduced from the Nancy, France nursery in the early twentieth century, valued for flower buds that open purple-flushed before fading to soft white on the face of each 1 1/4-inch bloom, with purple retained on the reverse of the petals. Dense clusters cover the arching branches in late spring, giving an airy, two-tone effect distinct from purely white-flowered deutzias. It grows into a larger, more upright shrub than dwarf gracilis types, so give it room in a mixed border or as an informal hedge. Prune immediately after flowering, removing a portion of the oldest canes each year, since bloom forms on the previous year's wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Alboaurea Japanese Forest Grass (Golden Ground-Covering Hakonechloa)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Alboaurea forms a dense, slowly spreading clump of deep yellow-and-green-striped shoots and colors best when shielded from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Set divisions or container plants in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, especially where summers are hot. Alboaurea makes gently arching, cascading hummocks of bright golden foliage striped with green, holding its color best out of direct midday sun. Growth is slow to establish but forms a dense, ground-covering mound over two to three seasons; top-dress with compost each spring and keep soil from drying out. Cut back matted foliage in late winter before new shoots emerge.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Samurai Japanese Forest Grass (Cream-and-Green Variegated Hakonechloa)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Samurai tolerates more light than most hakone grass cultivars but still benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil that tolerates some clay; Samurai adapts to full sun through partial shade, unusually flexible for a hakone grass, though foliage color stays cleanest with some afternoon shade in hot regions. Ribbon-like leaves emerge cream-white and green and pick up gold and burgundy tones as the season progresses, arching into refined, gradually spreading mounds. Green flower spikes appear in late summer and dry well for arrangements. Cut down old foliage in late winter before new growth begins, and divide congested clumps in spring.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
